#5809. Germany’s Hydrogen Pipeline Reached Marl. Its Market Still Needs to Add Up.

Germany’s hydrogen backbone achieved a genuine milestone on August 4, 2026. RWE and its partners announced that renewable hydrogen produced during commissioning at Lingen had reached Marl Chemical Park, roughly 120 kilometres away. Electrolysers, converted natural gas pipelines and industrial receiving infrastructure were working together.

The GET H2 consortium deserves credit for getting the equipment operating. But completing a hydrogen pipeline and establishing an economically competitive market for the hydrogen moving through it are different achievements.

The announcement did not disclose the quantity received at Marl, the price paid by an industrial customer or which existing hydrogen production was displaced. The English release describes hydrogen being available for industrial use, while the German release says it was used. Neither provides the industrial mass balance needed to determine the actual emissions benefit. The network also contained hydrogen from earlier commissioning activities, which makes tracing individual molecules through the pipeline less useful than measuring what changed at the receiving industrial facilities.

Marl is hardly a new hydrogen customer. The chemical park has used hydrogen for decades in integrated production processes. Providing another source may be useful, especially where renewable hydrogen replaces fossil-derived supply, but existing demand does not automatically become commercially viable demand for a considerably more expensive feedstock.

The larger infrastructure ambition makes that distinction important. Germany’s approved hydrogen core network covers 9,040 kilometres and has expected investment costs of €18.9 billion. Much of the network will use converted natural gas pipelines. These are approved plans and anticipated investments, not evidence that the entire network has been built or that future customers have committed to using it.

There are genuine industrial commitments. RWE has a 15-year agreement with TotalEnergies to supply approximately 30,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually to the Leuna refinery from 2030. That provides a named customer, volume and contract period. The price is undisclosed, and European fuel regulations help create demand for renewable hydrogen in refining.

That is a much stronger commercial signal than commissioning a pipeline. The question is how many comparable customers exist, what they can afford and whether their businesses will continue using hydrogen over the decades required to recover infrastructure investments.

The wider European outlook has become less optimistic. ENTSOG’s October 2026 draft assessment reduced its 2030 hydrogen demand assumption from 620 TWh to 335 TWh, a 46% reduction from its 2024 assessment. Its 2040 assumption fell 33%, from 1,929 TWh to 1,296 TWh. These are changes to European planning scenarios, not measurements of declining actual hydrogen consumption, but they matter when infrastructure economics depend on demand growth.

My central model of hydrogen supplied through the Lingen system produces an illustrative delivered cost of about €9.06/kg after assumed capital support, compared with a €3/kg conventional hydrogen benchmark. Those are scenario values, not RWE’s actual costs or the undisclosed price paid at Marl. The gap illustrates the challenge facing industrial manufacturers selling chemicals into competitive international markets.

Hydrogen remains an important industrial feedstock. Well-located connections between producers and customers with durable demand may be worthwhile. Germany needs evidence that the customers and products can support the investment, rather than assuming that building enough pipelines will bring the market into existence.

#5806. Swarm Of Electric Trucks Coming To US (Battery Swapping Included?)

Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously ditched the idea of EV battery swapping back in 2015 after a brief experiment. That pretty much laid the idea to rest here in the US, but other EV stakeholders soldiered on. The latest example is the Australian firm Janus Electric, which is bringing its Class 8 heavy duty electric truck conversions to North America. Janus offers a battery-as-a-service model that includes both charging and swapping…so, is battery swapping finally coming here to the US?.

Battery swapping for two-wheelers and larger EVs is commonplace in some overseas markets, with industry leader Nio being one example. So far, though, swapping stations for e-bikes are the only sign of emerging activity in the US.

Musk’s opinion aside, a modern battery swapping station can change a spent electric car battery for a fresh one in just a few minutes, or less time than it takes to drive through an automated car wash. On the other hand, considering today’s EV fast charging technology, battery swapping is somewhat less relevant to passenger cars and other light duty vehicles. Access to home charging is another factor that can limit the appeal of driving to a battery swapping station for a refresh.

Electric trucks, though, are another kettle of fish. Every minute counts in the fast paced transportation industry. Waiting in line for an EV charging station to free up is a non-starter, and then there’s the charging time. Even the much-heralded Tesla Semi Class 8 truck can take hours to reach a full charge overnight, though the truck is reported to achieve 60-70% charge in as little as 30-45 minutes at fast charging stations.

The time factor explains why battery swapping for trucks is appearing in overseas markets. The seeds of change have also begun to sprout up in the US, where the the diesel-to-electric conversion field is beginning to offer some opportunities. Last summer, for example, the US startup Revoy (formerly SixWheels) announced a swappable battery retrofit for Class 8 diesel trucks. The retrofit consists of a battery unit inserted between the cab and the trailer, which can be swapped out in a matter of minutes. The unit does not replace the engine, but it reportedly cuts diesel emissions by up to 85%, with a 95% fuel savings aided by regenerative braking.

The US Army is also dipping a toe in the conversion field with “idling kits,” which are batteries powerful enough to run on-board equipment for military vehicles in near silence, without the giveaway noise and heat signature involved in idling the vehicle’s engine. No word yet on whether or not swap-outs will be part of the picture, but the technology pieces are in place.

So much for the current state of affairs. Last week a full diesel-to-electric conversion opportunity suddenly appeared when the Canadian lithium-ion battery specialist Electrovaya announced a new $26 million diesel-to-electric supply agreement with the Janus that leverages Electrovaya’s proprietary “Infinity Battery Technology, a durable system compatible with daily swapping cycles for Class 8 trucks.

The $26 million agreement represents just the initial phase of orders for the US and Canadian markets. “Electrovaya has also agreed to invest approximately $1.4 million in Janus for up to 4.2 million shares, together with up to 6.3 million warrants,” Electrovaya noted, indicating a long term partnership allowing plenty of room for scaleup.

“Janus’s approach converts existing diesel prime movers to battery-electric operation and pairs them with swappable battery packs and Janus Charge & Change Stations, allowing fleets to exchange batteries in minutes rather than wait hours to recharge, and to electrify without the capital cost of purchasing new trucks,” Electrovaya explained (see additional coverage on CleanTechnica  here and here).

Janus’s footprint in North American is still tiny, at 118 truck conversion orders and commitments in the US and Canada combined. However, the firm’s business with Electrovaya should help ramp up the activity. Janus has already begun deliveries to Electrovaya, and Electrovaya has announced a major expansion of its North American manufacturing footprint. The showpiece is a production facility in Jamestown, New York covering lithium-ion battery cells, modules, and packs.  Start of operations is schedule for sometime next year.

With US President Donald Trump’s war in Iran continuing to elevate diesel costs, both Janus Electric and Electrovaya smell an end to the partisan war on EVs that rocked the US market after Trump took office in January of 2025. “Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale,” said Janus CEO and Managing Director Ben Hutt in a press statement.

“The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport,” Hutt added.

The CEO of Electrovaya, Dr. Raj Das Gupta, also underscored the potential for rapid scaleup. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations,” Gupta emphasized.

“Our strategic investment, together with the warrants, aligns us closely with Janus’s long-term growth,” Gupta also explained, with warrants referring to up to 6.3 million in contracts for future stock transactions.

If you’re wondering how much traction Electrovaya and Janus will gain in the US electric truck conversion space, that’s a good question considering Trump’s on-again, off-again trade wars with the upstairs neighbors.

The factory in New York State should help push matters along. As if on cue, over the weekend the White House also signaled that Trump is suddenly willing to call off his tariff dogs, potentially leading to a trade deal with Canda that could help accelerate activity in the US electric truck conversion field, among other areas.

On the other hand, the negotiations are described as achieving an early stage “concept” of a deal, which makes it seem more like a weak effort to gin up voter support for the Republican ticket ahead of Election Day on November 3. The concept of a deal could just as easily de-materialize by the morning of November 4.

Deal or no deal, Trump is scheduled to leave office in January of 2029 at the latest — peacefully this time, one hopes — opening up space for a new era of stability and mutual benefit in US-Canada trade relations.

In the meantime, keep an eye on Electrovaya for more activity in the electrification field, with or without help from the US market. In addition to supplying batteries for electric truck conversion, the company anticipates business in the fields of material handling, robotics, defense, and AI data center infrastructure.

Photo: The Australian firm Janus Electric has hooked up with Canada’s Electrovaya to accelerate the electric truck conversion field in North America, regardless of the sharp U-turn in US electrification policy (cropped, courtesy of Janus).

#5802. As Diesel Costs Surge for Farmers & Rural Businesses, Solar Offers a Lifeline

The cost of diesel fuel rose nearly 33% from 2025 to 2026, with some countries experiencing even higher price spikes. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, solar-powered equipment offers an attractive alternative.

On a dry hillside in Chamwino, central Tanzania, mango farmers used to watch their trees struggle through the long months without rain. Irrigation was technically possible: A diesel pump could lift water from a nearby borehole. But in practice, fuel was too expensive and too unpredictable for smallholders to run the system often enough. When diesel prices rose, farmers irrigated less, production dropped, and most households stayed locked into low-yield farming and razor-thin margins.

In 2021, a solar-powered pump and drip irrigation system replaced the diesel setup as part of a pilot project. Within one season, farmers reported that their mango production and average income from mango sales roughly doubled, as farmers could irrigate beyond the rainy season and manage their orchards more intensively. The technology change was simple—solar instead of diesel. But for farmers, it meant shifting from a fuel prone to wild price swings to an energy source they could rely on and afford.

Chamwino is not an isolated case. Across Africa and other regions, farmers, processors, and rural businesses are among the most exposed to diesel price spikes, like those happening right now. Because diesel powers irrigation pumps, generators, mills, and refrigerators, every price jump shows up as higher operating costs, thinner margins, and greater risk.

Distributed clean energy is emerging as one of the most practical ways to break that dependence.

While access to electricity has expanded significantly over the last 10 years, the reality is that diesel still powers much of rural life in places like sub-Saharan Africa. Only 33% of the rural population can access electricity. Even among those with power connections, frequent outages and poor quality have led farmers, processors, retailers, mines and telecommunications companies to rely on diesel generators for backup or primary power. An Energy for Growth Hub study estimated that 150–190 gigawatts (GW) of distributed diesel generator capacity was operating across Africa in 2024, compared with 268 GW of grid-connected capacity. Removing South Africa from the equation, Sub-Saharan Africa had nearly 1.5 times as much diesel generator capacity as grid-connected capacity. And diesel capacity exceeded grid capacity in at least 26 African countries.

The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability created by this “shadow power system.” The average global retail diesel price exceeded $1.50 per liter in the second quarter of 2026, 20% higher than the previous three months and 32.9% higher than a year earlier. In Africa, retail diesel prices rose by 25% on average across 42 countries between mid-January and mid-June 2026.

The regional average masks sharp differences between countries. In some, subsidies, tax cuts, and administered fuel prices have cushioned consumers from rising international prices, but at a cost to government budgets, especially in fuel-importing economies with limited fiscal space. Elsewhere, consumers have faced much larger increases at the pump. Diesel prices increased by 86% in Nigeria and more than 50% in Tanzania and Ethiopia from January to June 2026.

The effects extend beyond the cost of running generators. Diesel powers agricultural machinery, irrigation pumps, mills and refrigerators. Diesel-fueled road transport connects farms with suppliers and consumer markets. The impacts of the Iran conflict are already rippling through interconnected energy, fertilizer, trade and logistics networks, raising the costs of agricultural production and food distribution across Africa and elsewhere. Fertilizer prices have increased by 30-45% in several African markets since the conflict began, increasing the risk that farmers will reduce application rates, switch to other crops or miss their planting windows.

The effects are felt most acutely at the local level. For example, members of a women’s groundnut processing cooperative in Nigeria reported that rising fuel and fertilizer costs increased the price of raw groundnuts and groundnut oil by 33%. In Myanmar, which imports more than 90% of its fuel and relies predominantly on road transport, higher diesel prices have increased the cost of moving food and agricultural inputs, and have led to rising rice prices for consumers.

We already have better alternatives. Many locations are struggling with diesel-based irrigation, cooling and backup power, but solar and other distributed renewables can provide more affordable and reliable electricity than diesel-dependent systems.

The shift is already gaining momentum. In Africa, 17 GW of solar capacity will be installed in 2026 — a 45% increase from 2025, equivalent to approximately 100,000 panels installed each day. Much of the recent growth is happening outside large power plants: Roughly three-quarters of Africa’s solar growth between 2023 and 2025 came from distributed systems, as households and businesses sought alternatives to unreliable supply and diesel generation.

The benefits are already visible for some who have made the switch.

Ethiopia’s Berbere district, or woreda, is surrounded by four rivers, yet for years farmers could not use that water for irrigation. Limited access to electricity and the high cost and unreliability of petrol and diesel made pumping water from rivers to fields impractical, keeping production closely tied to rain-fed maize and teff. In 2025, WRI and partners installed two solar-powered water pumps to lift river water to irrigated plots. In the first production season, households involved in the project earned an average $709 from onion cultivation alone, compared with around $207 annually from maize and teff before the solar-powered pumps were installed. Farmers also reported being able to harvest more than once a year, plant surplus crops such as onions and chilies to increase their incomes, and make new investments in livestock and home improvements.

Similarly, when Kenya experienced its longest nationwide power blackout in 2023, one Nairobi hospital maintained critical services thanks to its solar-plus-battery storage system. For rural clinics and county hospitals, similar systems can ensure power even when the grid fails, without tying budgets to volatile fuel prices and expensive back-up diesel generators.

There’s huge potential for distributed clean energy to further break diesel dependence and improve livelihoods in places like rural Africa and elsewhere. Energy Access Explorer, an open online geospatial platform hosted by the WRI Polsky Energy Center, lets planners examine solar potential alongside grid networks, health facilities, schools, and farming communities. Bringing these layers together can help governments and practitioners identify where clean power could cost-effectively serve livelihoods and services that currently depend on diesel.

For example, Energy Access Explorer is already informing electrification planning in Ethiopia. The Ministry of Water and Energy, working with the World Bank, has used the platform to prioritize off-grid electrification through a results-based financing program. Our latest analysis reveals that about 12.6 million people in Ethiopia live in areas with high agricultural activity and high solar potential, but little access to grid-connected electricity. These areas could be assessed for solar-powered irrigation, processing, cooling and other services that could benefit from distributed clean power.

A Uganda analysis applies the same approach to health services. The map below shows 243 health facilities and approximately 4.6 million people living in areas with limited or no connection to electricity. Yet these areas do receive abundant sunlight, making them suitable for solar power. Used alongside data on facility electricity demand, existing supply reliability, and roof or land availability, the maps can help prioritize clean power investments for rural health services.

As diesel prices continue to swing wildly with every conflict and crisis, farmers, processors, and rural businesses pay the price, alongside governments that try to keep costs low through subsidies. It’s time for energy ministers, donors and financiers to look closely at where distributed clean power can viably replace diesel and direct their investments there. The latest Tracking SDG 7 report estimates that $21 billion is needed by 2030 to provide off-grid solar to the 398 million people for whom it is the least-cost electricity option—approximately 6 times the sector’s recent investment level!

Moving from energy crisis to energy security is ultimately about knowing where clean energy truly changes livelihoods. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, that starts with swapping diesel for solar.

By Dimitris Mentiss, Lead, Energy Access Explorer

This article is informed by research and insights from the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition. The Center harnesses analytical power, convening ability, and global expertise to help orchestrate a transition to a clean, abundant, affordable, and reliable energy future by overcoming critical barriers.

WRI is a global research organization that spans more than 50 countries, with offices in Brazil, China, Europe, India, Indonesia, and the United States. #5801. The Senate permitting bill holds promise but needs amendments

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Targeted changes can minimize the most negative consequences of the permitting bill’s overreaching provisions, writes former FERC Chairman Mark Christie.

Mark Christie is a former chairman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and former chairman of the Virginia State Corporation Commission, and is the director of the William & Mary Law School Center for Energy Law and Policy.

Every true compromise in a polarized legislature contains candy for each side, but also requires each side to swallow some hairballs. In the Senate permitting reform bill (SB 5653), the true permitting reforms hold a welcome potential to get needed infrastructure built faster. The transmission provisions, however — which are not permitting reforms at all — contain some provisions that are indigestible if you care about rising consumer costs and respect for historic state authority over utilities.

The bill’s best transmission provisions seek to ensure that large-load customers pay the full costs they impose on the grid. The worst transmission provisions, however, can be fixed with the amendments described below. Before considering these amendments, it is important to understand that the Federal Power Act for nearly a century has recognized a clear and logical division between state and federal authority over the power grid: The states have authority over the siting and permitting of all physical assets within their borders, including generation and transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has authority over the rates for interstate transmission services and wholesale power sales.

The current Senate bill blows up this century-old balance of authority by giving FERC the sweeping power to order a transmission line built in any state, without regard to the state’s own decision on the project or the opposition of the state’s residents who will be directly affected. Congress has enacted so-called “backstop siting authority” before, most recently in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in 2021, but Congress strictly limited the geographic reach of FERC’s backstop authority to narrow geographic corridors established by the U.S. Department of Energy and only after DOE made a finding that the national interest required the establishment of each corridor.

The Senate bill contains no geographic limits on FERC’s permitting power. It expands FERC’s authority to override the states to every square inch of the country, a breathtaking expansion of federal power at the expense of a core state function: the permitting and construction of utility assets within their own borders, projects that could have huge impacts on the lives of their residents.

Fortunately, targeted amendments can minimize the most negative consequences of the bill’s overreaching provisions. Here are three recommended amendments:

The bill allows FERC to order the construction of transmission lines based on a nebulous “public interest” standard. Such a standard is a blank check for FERC to approve trillions of dollars’ worth of transmission lines for whatever reason a presidential administration finds is in the “public interest,” as long as FERC adds general findings of some reliability improvements or consumer benefits, which can be claimed for every transmission line ever proposed. In the short term, FERC could use the bill’s grant of new authority to order transmission lines built to serve hyperscale data center development, a Trump administration priority. A future FERC could find that the public interest requires trillions of dollars of new transmission to meet “Net Zero” climate goals.

So my first recommended amendment is to remove the “public interest” and other general criteria, and instead require that FERC must find that the proposed line is the optimal solution to meet a proven reliability need at just and reasonable rates, compared to alternative solutions.

My second amendment addresses the critical role of states in cost allocation. FERC Order 1920 guaranteed to states in a multi-state region the right to reach an agreement on cost allocation for regional transmission projects and have that agreement submitted to FERC. The Senate bill should add an explicit guarantee that for regional transmission projects the states in each region have the right to agree on cost allocation and FERC shall presume such state agreement is just and reasonable.

My third amendment concerns one of the most onerous and frankly insulting provisions in the Senate bill. When we at FERC implemented the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act’s backstop siting authority, we gave each affected state one full year to conduct its permitting proceeding before FERC would start its own backstop proceeding. That allowed the state to develop a factual record and issue a decision within a reasonable period of one year.

The Senate bill allows FERC to start its backstop proceeding simultaneously with the state proceeding. That effectively renders the state proceeding meaningless, and states will perceive it exactly that way. Why should a state spend its time and limited resources on its proceeding when FERC is already doing its own? Any evidentiary record developed in the state proceeding may not even be available to FERC before it overrides the state. This provision in the Senate bill is nakedly punitive and overreaching and should be amended to give the states one full year to act before FERC can begin its own backstop proceeding.

Even if you don’t care about respecting state authority, you should care about the bill’s impact on consumers already struggling to pay their power bills. Over the past decade, transmission has been one of the fastest-growing drivers of power bill increases. The Senate bill as drafted could result in literally trillions of dollars of new transmission being ordered by FERC to serve whatever policy goals a president wants. These costs will flow right into consumers’ monthly bills.

Every compromise offers candy and hairballs. With these amendments, the bill can be made a lot sweeter.

#5799. The ETS Investment Engine: Scaling Europe’s Strategic E-fuel Market for Shipping & Aviation

Making the ETS a strategic investment tool for aviation and shipping

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) review proposal published in July 2026 is intended to make the EU’s most vital climate policy mechanism fit for its 2040 climate targets. It also carries the ambition to turn the ETS into an ‘’engine for innovation and investment”.

This policy brief looks at the investment dimension of the ETS proposal with respect to the aviation and maritime sectors. They are major contributors to the ETS revenue generation. We argue, however, that the proposed framework is not fit for purpose to adequately support clean fuel investments in these hard-to-abate sectors.

The ETS Review is an opportunity to set up a tailor-made investment tool to de-risk and boost the production and uptake of e-fuels, using the ETS funds from aviation and shipping. Early financial support is crucial for the development of a domestic e-fuels value chain, Europe’s geostrategic autonomy and the EU’s industrial position in the global competition for clean technologies. RFNBOs are the most scalable fuels needed to reach the targets under FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation.

#5796. Electric utilities join industries urging renewal of cybersecurity information-sharing law

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

CISA 2015, as the law is often called, provides liability protections for companies sharing cyber threat indicators amongst themselves and with federal agencies. It is set to expire next month.

Three dozen business groups, including organizations representing electric utilities and critical infrastructure sectors, are pressing Congress to renew a major cybersecurity information-sharing law before its expiration next month.

The 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act “has become a foundational component of the nation’s cybersecurity,” the groups wrote on Sunday to the chairs and ranking members of the congressional armed-services committees. Signatories included the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities, and the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association.

CISA 2015, as the law is often called, provides liability protections for companies sharing cyber threat indicators amongst themselves and with federal agencies. Those sharing alliances underpin the vast constellation of public-private collaboration groups that have sprung up over the past decade as the federal government has streamlined its approach to cyber defense.

After the law’s initial 10-year operating period expired in 2025, lawmakers passed several short-term extensions, with the latest one set to lapse on Dec. 11. Cybersecurity experts and industry leaders have repeatedly urged lawmakers to renew the law, calling it a critical tool for fighting hackers. Businesses now want Congress to include a new 10-year extension in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal year 2027.

“These authorities support the timely exchange of actionable threat intelligence and are central to the collective defense of public- and private-sector networks, particularly across critical infrastructure sectors,” the industry coalition wrote to lawmakers.

The signers include major trade associations representing almost every sector of critical infrastructure, including the Aerospace Industries Association, American Bankers Association, American Chemistry Council, American Petroleum Institute, Healthcare Leadership Council, National Association of Manufacturers, National Retail Federation, National Rural Water Association, U.S. Chamber of Commerce and USTelecom.

Cybersecurity-focused groups, including the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure and the Cybersecurity Coalition, also signed the letter.

Cybersecurity experts say the need for machine-speed information sharing has only grown as AI has sped up the pace of vulnerability discovery and cyberattack orchestration. In their letter, the business groups pointed to recent vulnerability crises that have led to global patching scrambles.

“In this environment, the speed and breadth with which defenders share information determines whether they keep pace with adversaries,” the industry coalition wrote. “That speed depends on the legal certainty CISA 2015 provides.”

The House’s draft version of the 2027 NDAA includes a provision reauthorizing and renaming the cybersecurity information sharing law. That provision would add AI to the list of topics about which companies can share information. The Senate’s draft NDAA does not include a CISA 2015 reauthorization.

Lawmakers will begin working to reconcile the two draft bills after they return to Washington on Nov. 9, following the midterm elections.

#5794. More of the Same Expensive Dependence on Fossil Fuels in TEP and APS 2026 Energy Plans

PHOENIX — Arizona utilities Tucson Electric Power Company (TEP) and Arizona Public Service (APS) filed their 2026 Integrated Resource Plans (IRPs) on Friday that evaluate how utilities will obtain energy for the next 15 years. While their plans include new renewable energy and storage, they continue to spend on fossil fuels, building new gas, and in the case of APS, extending coal use. Instead of facilitating a timely transition to affordable, clean energy, both utilities — and especially APS — continue an expensive dependence on fossil fuels that keep ratepayers in a dangerous cycle, paying the price for decades.

Arizonans already experience some of the highest electric bills in the country, with some of the most planned gas in the country. Yet, instead of easing energy burden and saving its customers millions of dollars, APS prolongs costly coal operations at the Four Corners coal plant, worsening climate impacts, increasing air pollution, and threatening public health.

Of all the state’s utilities, APS has the most planned fossil gas, adding over 4,000 MW of gas by 2041. APS’s gas projects include the planned Desert Sun Power Plant and the Redhawk Expansion Project, which includes constructing eight new methane gas-fired generating turbines in Maricopa County. It has also signed a coal supply contract extension to resuscitate its Four Corners Plant, abandoning APS’s previous plan to exit the plant in 2031 and instead extending coal-fired operations to 2038. In a pending case before the Arizona Corporation Commission, APS is also proposing a 14% rate hike that would increase the average residential customer’s utility bill by roughly $240 per year.

TEP’s energy plan includes coal to gas conversions of units 1 and 2 at its Springerville plant by 2031 rather than retirement of those units as TEP had previously proposed. TEP plans to exit its share of the Four Corners coal plant by 2031, but also plans to add 300 MW of new fossil gas generation. TEP had previously committed to reduce carbon emissions 80 percent by 2035 but now says in its plan that it won’t achieve that goal.

The public can submit comments on both utility energy plans. Both APS and TEP’s plans will come before the Arizona Corporation Commission to be approved or rejected.

“Arizonans across the state support a timely transition from fossil fuels to 100% clean energy by 2050, but what the utilities have presented in their energy plans further delays our move from gas and coal to solar and wind,” said Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr. “We’re seeing these utilities protect their own bottom lines, instead of making the most economical decisions for ratepayers like you and me. More than ever, we need to embrace a clean energy future to protect our health, the climate, and our wallets.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. #5791. They Are Trying to Silence Us

State and federal government officials are trying to harass, intimidate, and silence NRDC and other nonprofit environmental advocates.

The Attorney General of West Virginia recently initiated an investigation of NRDC and a handful of other groups on the stated ground that we may have committed consumer fraud. The theory appears to be that it’s deceptive for NRDC to say that the burning of fossil fuels contributes to climate change, which, in turn, causes harm to the planet and its people. But that’s fact, not fraud.

To pursue his investigation, the AG served a subpoena seeking a vast trove of confidential internal and external communications relating to our advocacy around climate change for the past 10 years. The demand could cover sensitive strategy memos for policy advocacy, draft comments on regulations, exchanges with coalition partners, back-and-forth among scientists, dialogues with donors, and drafts of NRDC publications; all disclosed to a hostile adversary.

Co-counseling with Democracy Forward, we responded to the subpoena by preparing a federal lawsuit asserting infringement of our First Amendment rights to speak, associate with others, and advocate for effective solutions to the climate crisis. Those solutions include the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable sources of energy. And that is what drives the AG’s attempt to punish NRDC: pure retaliation for the content of our point of view.

At 2:13 p.m. on October 22, we advised the AG that we were going to file suit early that evening. A little more than two hours later, at 4:32 p.m., the AG withdrew the subpoena.

The AG is not alone in trying to bully NRDC. In September, the Committee on Natural Resources of the U.S. House of Representatives sent a letter of inquiry to NRDC and 18 other nonprofit environmental groups, informing us they are investigating the groups’ litigation practices. Why? According to the Committee, the targeted groups “build powerful and profitable litigation machines funded by taxpayer dollars through the exploitation of statutory fee-shifting provisions.” On this purported basis, the Committee demanded that NRDC disclose an exhaustive array of intrusive information and documents that could take months of concentrated effort to produce.

The premise of the Committee’s inquiry is that NRDC “effectively function[s] as [a] law firm[] funded by taxpayer dollars.” It calls NRDC “one of the most active litigating environmental nonprofit organizations driving the exploitation of statutory fee–shifting provisions.”

While NRDC is indeed an active litigant in federal court, it rarely receives attorney fees from the federal government. During our past five fiscal years, NRDC’s income from such fees in cases involving agencies or statutes identified in the Committee’s letter constituted 0.112 percent of our operating budget. In light of this numerical fact, contending that NRDC “build[s] a business model focused on siphoning tax dollars by weaponizing litigation awards” is unmoored from reality. With minimal effort, Committee members or staff could have discovered this from documents in the public record.

Courts have repeatedly held that the citizen-based enforcement litigation NRDC conducts, which holds government agencies accountable to the law, is a public service, and that Congress meant to encourage such suits by providing the opportunity to recover fees when a court determines an award is appropriate. This is the paradox: The Committee, which is part of Congress, accuses NRDC of stealing taxpayer money, when NRDC is doing precisely what Congress itself has empowered and encouraged NRDC to do.

It is not the only paradox. The Committee claims that its purpose is “to root out waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer dollars.” If so, is it investigating the nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds the U.S. Department of the Interior has agreed to pay companies to abandon offshore wind projects that would produce economical, renewable energy? The government bought back the wind leases without any statutory authority to do so, drawing funds from the same pot of federal money that often covers attorney fee awards. The amount of taxpayer money expended on the buybacks during the past six months is more than 3,000 times the amount of attorney fees paid to NRDC over the past five years. To our knowledge, the Committee is not investigating the lease buybacks.

In response to the Committee majority’s attempt to intimidate NRDC, we sent this letter, asserting our First Amendment right to litigate to enforce the law. Thus far, the Committee has not sought to compel us to respond to its demand for documents.

The Natural Resources Committee has plenty of company within the House. The effort to harass environmental nonprofits and their funders is part of a multipronged attack that includes the House Committees on the Judiciary; Science, Space, and Technology; and Oversight and Government Reform. While NRDC is not yet a specific, named target of any of these additional House inquiries, other environmental nonprofits are.

These investigations and inquiries are designed to chill dissent, to punish those who disagree with the policies of those in power. The method of harassment is the same pernicious ploy we see repeatedly from the White House: Start with a lie (e.g., NRDC spreads deception, not facts, about climate change; NRDC feasts on federal attorney fees), then parlay the lie into a malicious attempt to deflect attention, divert resources, silence perceived enemies, and trample constitutional rights. It’s retaliation for protected speech. The West Virginia AG doesn’t want to debate the relative merits of renewable energy and fossil fuels—he wants to punish us because we disagree with him.

The recent moves by the West Virginia AG and the House Committees erode the rule of law. Not to speak out against them is to cede the narrative—to be complicit in a dangerous form of attempted repression. In the face of hostile questioning, the upright prosecutor Jack Smith recently told Congress that, while fear is contagious, so is courage. He’s right. Everyone who acquiesces in these abuses of government authority makes it easier for everyone else to do the same. Everyone who speaks out encourages others to resist.

It is not enough to survive this moment, silent and unscathed. As an organization rooted in the law, NRDC is compelled to fight for freedoms central to our democracy. The climate crisis is the existential issue of our day. But climate is not the only thing at risk.

We will persist without fear to address the ravaging effects of climate change and enforce the law against polluters. Our millions of members and supporters expect and deserve that from us. We did not succumb to intimidation, and we will not succumb to it if it comes our way again. This is the sole silver lining in the misguided attempt to bully NRDC into submission and silence: It will not work.

NRDC is the nation's most effective environmental action group, combining the grassroots power of 1.3 million members and online activists with the courtroom clout and expertise of more than 350 lawyers, scientists, and other professionals.

#5789. Trump ban on foreign grid components sparks industry concern over practicality, cost

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Stakeholders applauded the order’s intent to secure the grid but said restrictions based on geography, rather than function and capability, miss the point and threaten investment.

President Donald Trump’s recent executive order seeking to protect the bulk power system from foreign threats correctly identifies the risk of U.S. reliance on outside suppliers, but mitigating those risks without stalling the grid’s buildout or saddling ratepayers with even more costs will be tricky, stakeholders told Utility Dive.

Executive Order 14421, issued Aug. 26, gives Secretary of Energy Chris Wright the power to block the installation of foreign-produced equipment – “or any critical component, software, firmware, digital service, maintenance service, or remote-access capability associated with such equipment” – that poses an “undue risk” to national security, either through intentional sabotage or supply chain disruption.

It also gave the secretary the authority to order the removal and replacement of previously installed equipment.

The Department of Energy has until Dec. 24 to publish rules and regulations implementing the order. In September, DOE asked industry and other stakeholders to weigh in.

Their responses to DOE’s request show broad support for the intent of the order, but concern over how it will be implemented. A number pointed out that security standards, especially for software that would enable remote access, can be more important than country of origin since flaws in any system can be exploited by anyone, anywhere.

The vast majority of stakeholder responses that took a position on the “function over origin” question favored DOE emphasizing functional controls as opposed to a software product’s origin, according to data compiled by industry analyst Brendon Shank.

Many respondents also said they wanted DOE to take a phased approach to introducing new compliance rules and allow some vendors to “prequalify” as trustworthy. Utilities are projected to spend more than a trillion dollars on grid upgrades through 2030 and are racing to secure contracts for equipment amid rising manufacturer backlogs.

“Supply chains are already approaching a breaking point for many categories of electrical industry products,” said the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, which represents more than 300 electrical equipment manufacturers.

“[W]e strongly encourage the DOE to consider the time, money and resources it takes to evaluate, redesign, develop and produce equipment that is made for the electrical system,” it said. “At a time of high demand and longer lead times than during periods of more stable electricity growth, that is only further complicated by balancing timeliness with retooling or restructuring of production lines to meet new changes.”

Until DOE releases its determinations, the industry faces a lot of uncertainty and big questions, said Alice Wu, a manager of federal policy at the clean energy nonprofit RMI.

Even though the order instructs DOE to focus on transmission-related equipment and components of 69 kV or higher — not on the distribution system — it also puts distribution system components linked to the bulk system with questionably sourced software under scrutiny, she said.

“It is not feasible for generation, transmission and distribution providers to rip-and-replace every piece of equipment and for DOE to check it,” Wu told Utility Dive in an interview. “What is the secure proxy for that? … And what will the potential cost impacts to ratepayers be?”

The U.S. has imported more than $22 billion in bulk-power equipment since 2025, particularly from China, which would likely be the country most impacted by the order, according to a recent Wood Mackenzie analysis.

Transformers and substations are already in an estimated market shortage of 15% and 8%, respectively, in 2026, and “restrictions on the use of Chinese built units is going to further exacerbate the supply chain challenges,” WoodMac said.

The market for 100 MVA power transformers is particularly exposed, it said, adding that the market for power transformers greater than 10 MVA has expanded nearly 300% since 2020.

A different analysis by RMI and BloombergNEF said the value of grid imports in 2025 was more than $30 billion. Together, Mexico, Southeast Asia and the European Union made up more than half of that, while China accounted for $3.5 billion and “other” countries for $7.4 billion.

NEMA and other stakeholders and experts applauded the order’s emphasis on software, maintenance support and other services that introduce remote-access capabilities. They also pointed to existing security standards DOE could apply from the North American Electric Reliability Corp., the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and others.

“Overall, this executive order focuses on the right security areas because it makes those who deploy critical infrastructure accountable for their software,” said Aaron Rose, a security architect manager with Check Point Software Technologies, which assesses security for utilities and other companies.

Check Point sees an average of about 3,000 cyberattacks per large organization per week, he said in an interview with Utility Dive.

DOE software determinations will be complicated, because “almost everything on the power system is software defined, controlled and driven,” he added.

DOE could ask for a software’s source, who maintains it, who has remote access to it, and where updates originate, Rose said. But updates for most firmware, cloud control systems, substation systems and customer-owned devices are from open-source libraries or code already written for other uses, making their countries of origin difficult to identify, and eliminating all software of uncertain origin is impractical, he said.

Power system software may also be sub-contracted to a third-party, Rose continued. Hardware manufacturers may or may not have documentation on that software’s developer or on who has remote access for updates, or be able to trace them, even with AI tools.

To avoid a complicated decompiling by a security team and still ensure critical needs are met, DOE could require future updates and remote access to be from secure sources, he added.

Rose said it is unclear whether the costs for such measures will fall on software vendors, infrastructure owners or their consumers.

An analysis of the order by the Rainey Center, a policy think tank, also questioned the logic of restrictions based on geography rather than capability and function.

“The risks the order names travel through code, connections, and control, and they work the same whether a device is built abroad or at home,” it said. “A ban governs geography; a standard governs the risk, on every device.”

The report recommended DOE define risk by “a verifiable, technology-neutral standard” built on existing controls, as well as a system for vendors to prequalify through independent U.S. testing.

The order’s flexibilities, like phased compliance, can allow determinations that avoid negative economic impacts, said Danielle Russo, executive director of  SAFE, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on U.S. national and economic security.

DOE can provide power system manufacturers and developers the clarity they need with lists of the specific supply chain equipment and components that are secure, Russo said. That will avoid slowing manufacturing investment and project development needed to meet load growth, she added.

In today’s complex investment environment, uncertainties from tariffs to changing political leadership can threaten investors with stranded assets, Russo said, adding: “It is hard to blame them for being challenged by that.”

DOE’s security restrictions should be balanced with legislated incentives that provide long-term certainty, Russo said.

#5788. Participation in Sunrun’s Puerto Rico VPP program doubled in 2026

Sunrun announced that participation in its Puerto Rico distributed power plant has doubled to more than 60,000 customers, representing nearly 70,000 home batteries. The distributed power plant frequently and reliably delivers 45 MW of dispatchable power for four hours at a time, providing critical support to Puerto Rico’s electric grid.

Since April, Sunrun has dispatched its power plant more than 60 times to weather severe energy shortfalls and prevent rolling blackouts. During an extended period of unseasonably hot temperatures this fall, Sunrun dispatched its home batteries to the grid for 18 consecutive days beginning October 13.

Sunrun’s Puerto Rico distributed power plant has scaled rapidly since 2024, when approximately 4,000 customers were enrolled. Enrollment surged to more than 30,000 customers in 2025. Sunrun is the largest aggregator in Puerto Rico’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing program.

Puerto Rico’s electric utility operator, LUMA, said in June and again in July that energy from home batteries helped “maintain system stability and prevent outages that would have affected thousands of customers.”

“What began in Puerto Rico out of necessity for family resilience has become a vital blueprint for the U.S. mainland, where severe weather and the proliferation of AI data centers are demanding new energy solutions,” said Sunrun CEO Mary Powell. “Sunrun is uniquely positioned to provide these solutions, whether to support a grid at its breaking point or to provide capacity for hyperscalers looking to come online.”

Sunrun’s increased dispatching capacity in Puerto Rico comes after residents on the island experienced an average of 36 hours of power outages in 2025 that were not caused by major adverse weather, which is 19% more than the previous year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. When severe weather is factored in, residents experienced an additional 23 hours of power interruptions.

Customers who participate in Sunrun’s Puerto Rico distributed power plant choose how much energy to share, with most contributing a small portion of their total battery capacity. This approach ensures they retain reserve power for personal backup power in the event of grid outages. Participants are financially compensated for the power they choose to share, while Sunrun generates recurring revenue by operating the distributed power plant.

#5787. The Future of Buildings in Illinois Is Electric

The Illinois Commerce Commission authorized a study of the most affordable way for the state to meet its building decarbonization goals. The report has fundamental flaws but critical insights.

Illinois’s landmark Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) sets the goal of 100 percent clean energy across the state by 2050. For nonelectric sources of emissions and transportation—such as the 17 percent of emissions that occur when we burn gas to heat our homes and other buildings where we live, work, and play—CEJA provides little direction on how these sectors are expected to align with the state’s climate goals.

The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC), which regulates the state’s electric and gas utilities, showed real leadership in 2023 when it found that “if the decarbonization goals of CEJA are to be met, the gas distribution system as currently operated will need to change.” To chart that change, the ICC launched a Future of Gas (FOG) open stakeholder process to identify the most efficient, cost-effective path to a gas system that fits the state’s climate goals.

As part of this FOG process, the ICC authorized a consultant to model five pathways to that CEJA-compliant system by 2050. In its recently released Gas Decarbonization Pathways Study, the consultant modeled a range of scenarios, from one where the state invests heavily in energy efficiency and helps customers replace outdated gas appliances with high-efficiency electric alternatives to others that rely on unproven biofuels with no clear evidence that they can be produced at anything close to the scale needed. For each scenario, the consultant was expected to assess technical feasibility, up-front and operating costs, impacts on the gas and electric systems, emissions reductions, and effects on environmental justice communities, all to help Illinois meet its gas decarbonization goals at the lowest cost and with the most benefits to residents.

Unfortunately, the consultant’s final report is biased by faulty (and at times, plainly unrealistic) assumptions that do not allow for accurate comparison across scenarios. Despite this, the study yields a clear finding: Gas use in Illinois’s buildings and industrial facilities must decline by at least 50 percent in order to reach the state’s climate target of net-zero emissions by 2050. Together with the state’s recently released Comprehensive Climate Action Plan, the study offers Illinois policymakers a clear agenda for initiating the transition to an affordable, equitable, and clean energy future.

The study offers some useful insights, but treating all of its findings as a road map for Illinois’s gas transition would be a mistake. Before getting into the no-regrets steps that Illinois can take now, we need to unpack the biggest problems with the report, including the flawed assumptions behind some of its conclusions.

Despite the study’s shortcomings detailed above, several key findings should influence the recommendations in the final FOG report:

The remaining technologies are incredibly early-stage, and to the extent that they are available at all over the next several decades, they are likely to be extremely expensive. The study’s assumptions around e-methane are particularly troubling. Modeling initially showed that the Continued Gas Use and Hybrid Gas cases could not meet the net-zero-by-2050 emissions requirement using only available technologies, like biomethane. As a result, in the final report, the model selected e-methane to backfill any resource gap—despite the fact that e-methane derived from green hydrogen and direct air carbon capture is still in “prototype and demonstration stage” today.

While the pathways study acknowledges that “[h]igher-gas scenarios present … greater challenges in alternative fuel procurement, technology readiness, long-term affordability, and air quality” compared to electrification-focused scenarios, this is a significant understatement. Scenarios relying on e-methane are infeasible and should not be considered on equal footing with scenarios that primarily rely on electric heat pumps, which already comprise 47 percent of air conditioner sales and have annually outsold gas furnaces since 2021.

The pathways study reinforces the need for Illinois to proactively plan for a future where gas demand declines, which occurs under all five scenarios despite flawed assumptions that heavily favor continued gas use scenarios. The state can and must act now to achieve the state’s climate goals in an affordable and equitable way. Illinois does not need to solve every aspect of the transition in the next few years. However, it can begin taking the following no-regrets steps now to prepare for a changing energy landscape.

Despite its numerous flaws, the study underscores the transformative role that clean, electric heat pumps will play in Illinois’s energy future and the need to plan for a smaller gas system. The ICC and the state legislature can and must begin advancing no-regrets building electrification policies today to ensure tomorrow’s energy system is healthy, clean, and affordable for all of the state’s residents.

By Madeline Semanisin, Policy Director, Illinois, Climate & Energy, NRDC; and Kiki Velez, Equitable Gas Transition Lead, Climate & Energy, NRDC

#5786. APS expects sales to double by 2041, plans extending coal use to 2038

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Peak demand will grow about 3.4% annually over the next 15 years, driven by industry and data centers, Arizona Public Service said in an integrated resource plan filed Friday with regulators.

APS projects peak demand of more than 14.5 GW in 2041, almost 60% higher than its current record peak of about 9.2 GW, set in August. And the utility expects annual retail sales to grow to about 80,600 GWh in 2041, up from about 34,200 GWh in 2025.

There is some uncertainty behind APS’ load projections, but the utility said it has taken steps to protect customers.

Despite refinements to APS’ large-load interconnection process, the “sustained record levels of interest” from large customers poses “a risk in increased potential for unrealized loads,” APS said in its resource plan, which it files every three years with the Arizona Corporation Commission. To mitigate the risk, APS said it adopted strategies such as having customers commit to “minimum demand and energy-based contract terms, providing collateral in case of default, and instituting early exit fees.”

As a result of population growth and higher levels of economic activity, APS said it expects to add up to 29,000 residential customers annually in the near term, and across the planning period the utility anticipates annual customer growth to be in the range of 1.5% to 2.5% through 2030.

The utility’s preferred plan includes continuing to operate the Four Corners coal plant beyond a planned 2031 retirement. APS said the extension could save customers close to $1 billion.

“The company will continue to evaluate the appropriate time to cease operations between 2031 and 2038, with the decision depending on customer needs, economics and other factors evaluated through future planning processes,” APS said in a statement.

“Reliability is nonnegotiable,” Mike Eugenis, APS director of resource planning, said in a statement.

APS’ planned natural gas resource additions include repowering the Cholla Power Plant as a 387-MW facility by 2030, adding 1,107 MW through new combustion turbines at existing APS sites and uprates to tolling units during 2026-2030, according to the IRP. Under the plan, APS will also add the 1,238 MW Desert Sun combined-cycle facility in 2032 to serve large-customer subscription load.

Customer and clean energy advocates were critical of the APS plan.

APS’ proposal “further delays our move from gas and coal to solar and wind,” Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr said in a statement. “We’re seeing these utilities protect their own bottom lines, instead of making the most economical decisions for ratepayers.”

The utility “should be investing in proven community-based energy solutions, like local solar and battery storage,” Vote Solar West Senior Regulatory Director Kate Bowman said in a statement.

APS “failed to consider how alternative technologies like rooftop solar, battery storage, and other distributed resources could help meet energy needs,” Bowman said. As the ACC considers the plan, regulators will have “an opportunity to push for a more comprehensive approach that puts affordability, reliability, and the interests of customers at the center of long-term planning,” she added.

The utility said it is adding nearly 2 GW of renewable utility-scale solar and 2.5 GW of battery storage in the next two years, “diversifying our resources to keep energy reliable and affordable.” By 2030, APS said it expects to have approximately 6 GW of battery storage on its system.

The utility also expects continued growth in customer-sited resources. APS said behind-the-meter storage adoption is expected to grow every year to 1.2 GW by 2045 — up from 69 MW today. For 2032, the storage forecast is approximately 95% higher compared to the last storage forecast developed in 2023, APS said.

Behind-the-meter solar adoption is expected to slow relative to the 2020-2023 period but “will still experience some modest growth,” reaching 3.7 GW by 2045 — up from 2.1 GW today.

Electric vehicles in APS service territory are expected to grow from 65,000 vehicles today to 1.1 million in 2045, resulting in 5.2 TWh of EV charging load, APS said. In 2042, this forecast is approximately 18% lower compared to the last EV forecast developed in 2023, it noted.

#5785. US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Amid a challenging market environment, the report shows that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of new wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

“The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”

Power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

The five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, New Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

Wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

“U.S. offshore wind shows diverging momentum,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

“U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”

#5784. Congress Is Cutting Off Transportation Investments that Help Families Save Money

The loss of guaranteed federal funding could stall projects that make it easier and cheaper for Americans to get where they need to go.

UPDATE: On October 27, 2026, an update to the Senate Commerce Committee’s Chopping Block report provided a state-by-state assessment of the harm to transportation systems if Congress fails to renew the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s $36.8 billion in advance appropriations funding. Led by Ranking Member Cantwell, the report demonstrates that these cuts will only drive increased costs for families and business across the country.

At a time when Americans are struggling to pay staggering prices at the fuel pump and the Trump administration sows uncertainty for states and communities by clawing back committed transportation infrastructure funds, Congress is moving to scale back more critical federal funding for affordable and clean transportation.

The need for consistent funding is clear: Transportation costs are the second-largest household expense in the United States, and our roads and transit infrastructure remain structurally inadequate. Nevertheless, state transportation and transit authorities are facing a significant funding cliff due to the expiration of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) on September 30, 2026. Over the past five years, the infrastructure law has provided a guaranteed pot of funding worth $36.8 billion for transportation projects. These “advanced appropriations” cover a wide breadth of programs and include large amounts of funding for clean transportation, such as electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure projects, transit, and rail investments. This funding has helped state transit and transportation authorities plan for longer-term projects and has been critical to the infrastructure law’s support of almost 70,000 unique transportation projects across the country.

But transportation funding from the infrastructure law ran out on September 30, 2026, and while Congress passed a short-term extension until December 11, 2026, it does not include these guaranteed dollars. This means that, for the three-month duration of the extension, states will lack the continuity and certainty they need to plan for both large- and small-scale infrastructure projects.

To add insult to injury, Congress also seems to be contemplating leaving this guaranteed funding out of the next transportation bill altogether. The House BUILD America 250 Act proposal, released in May, proposes cutting all advanced appropriations funding. The proposal, in fact, slashes transportation funding from current infrastructure law levels by almost 50 percent, leaving Americans without access to travel options that help defray rising costs.

Historically, transportation bills have included authorizations of two types of funding: (1) contract authority, which is supported by revenues that flow into the Highway Trust Fund and (2) general funds, which Congress has to “appropriate” and assign annually. The current infrastructure law includes another category—advanced appropriations—which makes money available in the future for certain programs without the need for any congressional action in future years, guaranteeing states and communities secure funding over the five-year bill period. This certainty allows for states to plan in advance for future projects and grant opportunities.

Any cut to this pot of money takes a sledgehammer to clean transportation programs that reduce household costs and improve the health of our communities. Particular programs at risk include the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, which helps states build a national network of EV chargers; the Capital Investment Grants, a transit-related discretionary grant program; and the Reconnecting Communities Pilot, which aims to address harms caused by past transportation decisions. Also of concern are the BUILD and MEGA grants, which help support the build-out of transit, bicycle, and pedestrian infrastructure.

Congress is unlikely to agree on a new bill before the current extension comes to an end in December 2026, meaning that there is an opportunity to include advanced appropriations in any future extension of the current infrastructure law and the next transportation bill so that states and local governments can avoid having to grapple with temporary or potentially even permanent funding interruptions. This guaranteed funding is even more important now as transportation decision-makers contend with the Trump administration interfering with implementation and funding guidance. Additional funding clawbacks will only serve to stall progress. The sustained funding will also allow states and local governments to continue to build on the progress that the current infrastructure law made on clean transportation investments.

Even more important, American households are currently struggling to afford their basic daily necessities, and soaring gas prices have left many searching for ways to save on their transportation costs. In 2024, when gas prices averaged below $3.50 a gallon (a far cry from the current average price of $4.35 a gallon), transportation was the second-largest cost for American households, averaging 17 percent of household budgets. Cutting advanced appropriations funding for transit, EV charging, and rail will only serve to penalize the very households struggling the most, at a time when those investments would give Americans access to a wide range of affordable, reliable, and safe transportation options.

By Shruti Vaidyanathan, Director, Transportation Advocacy, Climate & Energy, NRDC

#5783. $150 Billion More Paid by Americans for Gas This Year Than Last

Since the beginning of America’s war against Iran, Americans have paid an additional $150+ billion for gas and diesel than they did last year during the same time period, according to a study from Brown University. Global gas prices have risen because supply has been disrupted (Iran having one of the top oil reserves in the world). Americans are paying upwards of $6 a gallon even though American oil companies have not had their own supply chains disrupted the way crude from the Middle East has.

The result? Windfall profits for big oil at the expense of American citizens.

In the leadup to his election in 2024, Donald Trump asked about 20 oil executives at Mar-a-Lago to raise $1 billion for his campaign, promising to reverse dozens of Biden-era regulations if elected. The industry seems not to have raised the full $1 billion, but oil interests still gave tens of millions to Trump-aligned committees. The policies put in place by the Republican party, who has had control of congress and the White House since the last election, have been very pro oil & gas, whether they were anti-EV, anti-solar, anti-energy efficiency, anti-fuel efficiency, anti-wind, or just flat out subsidies to oil and gas.

They ended many of the Biden Administration’s clean energy policies. They ended the Solar For All Program (or tried to). They ended residential and commercial solar tax credits. They signed Executive Order 14315 to terminate wind and solar production and investment tax credits and impose additional restrictions. They made solar development on Federal lands more difficult. On his first day in office, Trump signed a memo withdrawing federal offshore areas from new and renewed wind leasing – but the rule didn’t apply to oil and gas. They ended wind tax credits. They kneecapped the federal standards for vehicle fuel efficiency. They tried to eliminate Energy Star, a program that costs the government $32 million a year and saves Americans $14 billion a year. They weakened Home Energy Rebate programs, SPECIFICALLY stipulating that they could not be used to replace polluting gas furnaces (that increase childhood asthma by more than 15%) with energy efficient electric options. They even tried to make it illegal for future legislators to improve energy efficiency legislation. Then, as if that wasn’t enough, they just gave our tax dollars to the fossil industries, allocating about $190 billion in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade from the OBBBA.

If this isn’t quid pro quo, I guess I don’t understand what quid pro quo is. But the Iran War took it to a whole new level.

Since it began on February 28, as Americans have spent about $150 billion more on gasoline and diesel, U.S. oil and gas companies earned more than $130 billion in profit from April through September, nearly triple what they earned a year earlier, according to the New York Times.

We can’t say the war was fought for the industry. The president has said his focus is stopping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. But we can say who is paying at the pump and who is collecting.

Connect the dots however you like, but connect them before you vote. Add it to the roughly $50 billion that US taxpayers have directly spent on the war, and untold more that has percolated through the rest of our economy due to inflationary pressure from rising energy costs, and it’s safe to say it’s well over $200 billion that this war has cost us, alongside the unquantifiable cost in human lives and suffering.

Wars fought for oil are nothing new. But there are things about this conflict that are new.

Oil shocks focus the mind, and this week’s reporting shows how fast the world outside the US is moving to get away from oil dependency. CleanTechnica’s analysis argues that global oil demand is on track to fall by 2–3 million barrels a day this year, the first drop not caused by a recession or pandemic, as high prices push consumers away from fuel. You can see it in China, where gas-car sales fell 49% in September and EVs hit a record 67% share. Europe is also answering, with affordable small EVs like the Smart #2 and an electric Citroën 2 CV at about €15,000. In Australia, a Chinese-built electric semi is already hauling cement for about half the price of its rivals, and Africa’s e-mobility leaders are talking about building vehicles rather than just importing them. Drivers who’ve switched are happy too: 82% of XPeng owners in a 4,000-person European survey said they’d recommend the brand, versus a 53% average.

Every driver, trucker, and country that electrifies becomes less exposed to the next oil shock. The question for the U.S. is how fast it joins in. And this election will go a long way toward answering that question.

Scott Cooney (LinkedIn) is a serial eco-entrepreneur focused on making the world a better place for all its residents.
