#5683. Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s

Some people have the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease but never develop dementia. While others experience worsening memory and thinking problems, these individuals remain mentally sharp despite signs of the disease in their brains. Scientists have long struggled to explain why.

Now, researchers at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience have uncovered a promising clue. Their findings suggest that a rare group of brain cells, known as immature neurons, may behave differently in people who resist Alzheimer's symptoms. Rather than simply replacing damaged cells, these neurons could help protect the brain from the harmful effects of the disease.

This remarkable ability is known as cognitive resilience. It describes how some people maintain their memory and thinking abilities even when their brains show signs of damage or disease.

"Around 30 percent of older adults who develop Alzheimer's disease never experience its symptoms," says Evgenia Salta, senior author of the research. "We really don't know why. That's a big mystery, and a very important one."

Understanding this mystery could transform how scientists approach Alzheimer's, shifting attention from what causes brain cells to deteriorate toward what allows certain brains to remain healthy and functional.

One possible explanation for cognitive resilience is that some brains have a greater ability to repair or protect themselves as Alzheimer's progresses.

"Perhaps they can add new brain cells to a network that is degenerating," Salta says.

This possibility involves a biological process called adult neurogenesis, which refers to the production of new nerve cells (neurons) in an adult brain. Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, allowing us to think, learn, remember, and respond to our surroundings.

Scientists have established that adult neurogenesis occurs in several animal species. Whether it continues to happen in the adult human brain, however, has been a subject of scientific debate for decades.

If the human brain can produce new neurons later in life, those cells might help maintain important connections as aging and disease damage existing networks. However, finding immature neurons does not necessarily prove that they were recently formed.

To investigate this possibility, Salta and her colleagues examined donated human brain tissue obtained through the Netherlands Brain Bank, a research resource that collects and preserves brain samples.

The researchers compared three groups: people without detectable brain pathology, patients who developed Alzheimer's dementia, and individuals whose brains showed Alzheimer's pathology but who remained cognitively resilient.

The team concentrated on a small region within the brain's memory center, an area believed to be among the few locations where new neurons might develop.

Finding the relevant cells was far from straightforward.

"These cells are extremely rare, so we had to develop new ways to find them," Salta says. "We really zoomed in on the exact spot where we expected them to be."

The researchers also developed new approaches to analyzing their data, allowing them to identify the cells more precisely without relying heavily on assumptions drawn from animal studies.

Scientists Find Immature Neurons in Brains Over 80

The search revealed something remarkable. Immature neurons were present across all three groups, including in the brains of older adults.

These cells resemble neurons that have not yet fully matured, suggesting that the aging brain may retain cellular features associated with development and adaptability.

"Even at an average age of over 80, we still found these immature neurons in all groups," Salta says.

But the most intriguing discovery came when researchers compared the brains of people who had developed dementia with those who had remained mentally sharp despite Alzheimer's pathology.

Initially, the scientists expected resilient individuals to have substantially more immature neurons. If these cells help replace damaged neurons, having greater numbers might explain why some brains withstand the disease.

Instead, the difference in cell numbers was much smaller than anticipated.

That unexpected result pointed toward another explanation. The important distinction might not be how many immature neurons a brain contains, but how those cells respond when the brain comes under attack.

A Hidden Defense Against Alzheimer's Damage

When the team examined the activity of immature neurons more closely, they identified striking differences between the groups.

In cognitively resilient individuals, the cells showed signs of activating biological processes associated with survival and protection against damage.

"In resilient individuals, these cells seem to activate programs that help them survive and cope with damage," Salta says. "We also see lower signals related to inflammation and cell death."

Inflammation is part of the body's normal defense system, but when it becomes persistent in the brain, it can contribute to damage and interfere with communication between neurons. Cell death, meanwhile, gradually disrupts the networks responsible for memory and thinking.

The findings suggest that immature neurons in resilient brains may be better equipped to withstand these harmful conditions.

More surprisingly, their role might extend beyond protecting themselves.

"It might not be (only) about replacing lost neurons," Salta explains. "It could be that these cells support the surrounding tissue and help the brain stay functional and 'youthful'. They may act as a sort of fertilizer in a garden that has started falling apart."

In other words, rather than serving only as replacements for dying neurons, immature cells could potentially help maintain the environment surrounding existing brain cells.

Such support might allow neural networks to continue functioning even as Alzheimer's related damage accumulates.

Why Scientists Are Cautious About the Discovery

Although the results offer an intriguing explanation for cognitive resilience, Salta emphasizes that the researchers have not established exactly what these immature neurons do.

Their conclusions about the cells' possible protective roles are based on patterns observed in brain tissue, not direct experiments demonstrating those functions.

"We assume the cells' function based on the data, but we cannot confirm it in this type of study," she explains.

That distinction is particularly important because research on adult neurogenesis has attracted considerable public attention, sometimes leading to claims that go beyond what scientists have demonstrated.

The presence of immature neurons does not establish that new neurons are continuously being produced in older humans, nor does it prove that these cells are responsible for preventing dementia.

Other biological mechanisms almost certainly contribute to cognitive resilience as well.

"This is one piece of a very large puzzle," Salta concludes. "There will never be just one factor that explains resilience."

Could Alzheimer's Research Shift Toward Protecting the Brain?

The findings raise a broader question about aging: Why do some people's brains remain relatively stable while others experience progressive cognitive decline?

"Somewhere along this trajectory, there's a kind of decision point," Salta explains. "Some people remain stable, others develop dementia. We want to understand what drives that difference."

To explore this further, the researchers plan to investigate how immature neurons communicate and interact with neighboring brain cells. Understanding those relationships may reveal whether the cells actively contribute to resilience and how their protective responses might work.

The research also reflects a growing change in how scientists think about Alzheimer's disease.

Traditionally, much of the field has focused on understanding the processes that damage the brain, including the accumulation of abnormal proteins and the loss of neurons. Increasingly, researchers are also asking why some brains remain functional despite those changes.

By identifying the mechanisms behind this natural resistance, scientists hope to uncover new ways to preserve memory and cognitive abilities as people age.

"Cognitive resilience is extremely exciting," Salta says. "If we understand what protects these brains, it could eventually lead to new therapeutic strategies."

Although practical treatments remain a distant possibility, the discovery suggests that even in old age, the human brain may possess protective abilities that scientists are only beginning to understand.

#5682. Opinion: I moved to Europe for free health care. I miss my patient portal

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio.

Tuesday, at exactly 7 a.m., I arrived at my general practitioner’s office, in the basement level of his house, two blocks from mine in Mellieħa, Malta. There are six chairs in the waiting area. Ikea, I think. People note who got there first and go in, in turn. On his desk, there’s an ancient laptop with a big monitor running a vaguely Y2K version of Windows. He wears a digital Casio watch I remember my dad having in the 1980s. My American doctor’s office had a water feature.

My Malta doctor does bloodwork by appointment only, Tuesdays at 7 a.m. You tell him in advance what you need, and he has the tubes ready, hand-labeled with your resident number. The tubes are tracking the two diseases I brought with me. The number is what gets you into a socialized system that spends a quarter of what America costs per person and still has an average life expectancy of five more years. It’s not the Mediterranean diet doing the work. Malta has the highest obesity rates in adults in all of the E.U.

While I sat there, gauze pressed on the vein that just held the needle, he filled out a form for the lab, correcting an error with white-out tape. You can buy that down the street at the store that sells water shoes and postcards.

I left the United States for a variety of reasons, including that you can swim in the Potomac but shouldn’t. You can bask in the Mediterranean and should. But mostly, it was a calculation about health care. American medicine saved me, literally, more than once. My care was extraordinary, and it was also about to become extraordinarily unaffordable. I pay 38 euros a week here — about $2,300 a year — and it covers me and my medications, including the one that costs $80,000 per year in the U.S.

My medical resume is diverse. I’ve had multiple sclerosis since 2002. I had breast cancer. I have half a liver. I once broke my leg in three places — while standing still. In my adult life I have hit the catastrophic out-of-pocket maximum nearly every year.

Like most insured Americans, I had coverage through my employer, and later through my husband Brian’s employer, the federal government. My doctors were department heads at Georgetown and Johns Hopkins. The surgeon who repaired my leg did his residency at the Hospital for Special Surgery, the top-ranked orthopedic hospital in the country. I got him because he was on call. My post-mastectomy plastic surgeon had once chaired the board that certifies plastic surgeons. All of them. For the whole country.

Every visit was a $40 copay. Self-referral. My maximum out-of-pocket was $6,000. The plan cost $26,888 a year — Brian paid $9,988 and his employer paid the rest. We never thought about it.

Then came DOGE, which was clearing out the federal workforce in the name of preventing waste, fraud, and abuse. Brian worked for an Inspector General’s office that investigated and prosecuted … waste, fraud, and abuse.

He never got fired. But we didn’t want to live in the risk. He wanted to move into consulting, which meant buying insurance on the exchange.

I am an insurance company’s nightmare. Federal law currently says they have to take me. To be extra safe, we planned to go to New York, where Brian’s family lives, because preexisting conditions are written into state law.

The cheapest mid-level plan, including copays and deductibles, ran about $30,000 for the year for both of us. That was the 2026 number. Open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs Nov. 1 to Dec. 15. That’s a shorter timeframe than previous years, and marketplace premiums are up an average of 26% for 2026. United Healthcare is requesting a 52% increase for New York for 2027. Millions of Americans are running the numbers now.

Two incomes down to one. Our health care costs tripling from what we paid with Brian’s job. After a lot of thought and a single Excel spreadsheet, we decided our best option wasn’t New York after all. My mother, long dead, ended up being the deciding factor.

My mother left me an E.U. passport. That is not a financial plan or a policy proposal or anything I earned — it is an inheritance like my green eyes and forehead veins, and it is the only reason any of what follows was available to me. Most Americans with a condition like mine don’t have an escape hatch to the European Union. I did. And I had been claiming socialized medicine was ideal — the way! — for decades without ever having participated in it.

My social security contribution — that 38 euros a week — gives the entitlement.

Hospital stay in Malta? Free. Emergency helicopter rescue? Free. There is no prior authorization. No requirement to fail a cheaper drug before getting a better one. Nobody has sent me the letter I used to get every year from my U.S. insurer, announcing they would not cover my medication because they believed I had a secondary insurance policy I have never had. Every. Single. Year.

At least twice a year, my doctor would be on the phone yelling at an insurance company for denying coverage. There are people whose entire job it is to file those appeals. According to a 2025 AMA survey, U.S. doctors average 40 prior authorizations per week, and their practices spend 13 hours a week on them. Forty percent of doctors employ staffers just to deal with insurance companies. And about three-quarters of physicians report that denials have increased over the past five years.

To be honest, in Malta, I pay for medical care all the time. I just pay differently.

There’s a two-tiered medical system. Public and private. The care is guaranteed. Speed and convenience live wholly in the private tier.

I can walk into almost any pharmacy in Malta and see a GP operating privately that same day for 15 to 20 euros. A specialist is 70 euros. Always cash. Sometimes you get a receipt. An ultrasound — if you want it fast — is 120 euros. Mine was performed by a doctor specializing in breast cancer imaging. No tech. No radiologist to read it later. I got the report at the appointment.

Most specialists here see patients both publicly and privately, and many private appointments happen inside pharmacies. There are tiny offices tucked in the back or upstairs. My neurologist works in a hospital one day a week. The other four days he works in four different pharmacies. You pick the one closest to where you live or work or shop. When I asked him why the system works that way, he said, literally, “to make it convenient for the patients.” There is no lease, no waiting room, no receptionist, and no billing department because there is nothing to bill. You pay at the counter where the eye drops are.

In Attard, where I see him because it’s closest to my house, he works Tuesday mornings alongside a gynecologist, a nephrologist, and an ophthalmologist. The next day will be a different group. Malta has more than 200 licensed community pharmacies, dispensing medical care alongside prescriptions, sunscreen, nail polish remover, a surprisingly robust collection of perfumes, and subpar dental floss. I ship that in from the U.K.

When I needed an oncology checkup, I found Dr. Brincat, who ran the oncology department at Mater Dei Hospital for 17 years. I called a private clinic where he works now. They checked his schedule, called me back the next day, and gave me an appointment just two weeks out.

He scanned (visually, not electronically) more than 100 pages of my records. Other than the paper on his desk, there was a stethoscope. No computer. No iPad. No phone. He ordered a hormone panel to see whether I should switch from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor — something my American oncologist had said we’d get to at some point. They were in agreement on the protocol.

He ordered an ultrasound, handwriting a referral on letterhead and sealing it in an envelope from his top desk drawer.

It feels like time traveling back to the ’80s. But I’ve never had a doctor who needed to prove I needed anything. And a bill? Never seen one.

The private tier is easy. The public tier is where my medical fluency in the U.S. didn’t translate. I have to plan for things I never considered before. Like the speed of mail.

Before Dr. Brincat, I tried to do it the correct way, or rather, the free one. My GP requested a referral, and I was told to watch the mail for an appointment slip. The time you are given is not negotiable. The time is the time. The slip should arrive in roughly two weeks following the request.

I waited. When I called, they said they were still looking for a time for me.

The horror story Americans tell about socialized medicine is the wait. If you need a hip — good luck, check back in three years.

A friend of mine recently went from hip pain to a bad X-ray to a new hip in under 10 weeks in America. She also has excellent insurance, which is the entire sentence. America is the fastest system for some of its people. For the uninsured, the wait is not a year or three. It is indefinite.

I wasn’t prepared for the Maltese system paperwork, emphasis on the paper. To get my medication free, the Pharmacy of Your Choice program required proof that I had paid into social security — because there is no centralized system that simply shows that … I have. Buy a printer/scanner. You will need it.

I scanned and sent my receipts. They replied:

Thank you for contacting the POYC Schedule V office. This is to acknowledge receipt of your email. We will reply to your email in due course.

I have four similar messages in a folder named “Bureaucracy Stuff.”

After three weeks of due course, I called. My form had been mailed, they said, and must have been lost. They would mail it again. I could expect it in 10 business days. I asked whether I could just come get it. They said yes, they were open until 1 p.m. It took me 32 minutes, door to door, in heavy traffic.

In America, there is paperwork to prove you deserve a drug or surgery or treatment because the insurance company doesn’t want to give it to you. In Malta, there’s paperwork because there are forms and they are still on paper.

I have not received reminder texts here. No confirmation calls. I think I have a dermatologist appointment next week. Am I sure? No. I will show up and hope.

I worry that if my cancer comes back, I won’t have what I would have had in the U.S. The doctors are good here. But the bench isn’t as deep.

There are more MS drugs available in America than here — but not the one developed for my subtype. Tolebrutinib, sold as Cenrifki, is the drug American patients lobbied hard for. The Food and Drug Administration rejected it over risk of severe liver injury and questions of efficacy. The European regulator approved it in June. It’s the first drug shown to reduce disability in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS, and I’m in that group, and there is nothing else.

But it won’t come to Malta soon. Just because E.U. approved it doesn’t mean it gets to Malta because there aren’t enough patients to warrant it. There are more people with MS in the United States — nearly a million — than there are people in my entire country.

I did learn recently that there is a portal for the public system. For the private system, I keep a folder on my phone of photographs of my doctors’ notes. One of them is a lonely piece of paper under a stethoscope.

I have never received a bill here. I have no idea what a day in the hospital costs.

My neurologist and I are discussing a minor surgery — one overnight stay — to implant a device that delivers medication directly to my spinal cord. He told me we won’t get to choose the size, even though I would want the smaller one.

“It’s free,” he said, “so we don’t get as much say.”

Mariska Breland is a co-founder of The Neuro Studio, which provides movement education for people with neurological conditions and training for the professionals who work with them.

#5681. Voters Back Abortion Rights and Transgender Restrictions in Some States

— Measures provided a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election

Abortion-rights advocates notched victories in several states Tuesday, and voters in some states backed transgender restrictions as they decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states.

The ballot measures provided a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election in which Democrats took control of Congress and gained power in state legislatures and gubernatorial offices.

Voters defeated a proposed amendment to Missouri's constitution that would have reimposed restrictions on most abortions. The vote Tuesday essentially reaffirmed voters' decision from 2 years ago, when they became the first in the nation to undo an existing abortion ban by approving an abortion-rights amendment.

The Republican-led Legislature then referred a new, less restrictive version of an abortion ban to this year's ballot. The measure would have allowed abortions only for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, or in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. It also would have amended the constitution to prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.

Abortion-rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, heavily outspent abortion foes in a successful campaign to defeat the Missouri ballot measure.

In Virginia, a voter-approved measure creates a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" in the state constitution, ensuring that abortions can occur during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. The amendment also creates a right to contraception and fertility care, among other things.

An amendment approved in Nevada creates a fundamental right to abortion until fetal viability, which is generally considered after 21 weeks of pregnancy. The amendment won initial voter approval in 2024 but needed a second vote this year to add it to the constitution.

Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a nationwide right to abortion in 2022, voters in more than one-fifth of the states have passed ballot measures protecting abortion rights.

But voters in Republican-leaning Idaho on Tuesday defeated a ballot measure that would have created abortion rights in state law. Current Idaho law bans abortions unless necessary to save the life of a pregnant woman, or during the first trimester of pregnancy in cases where rape or incest has been reported to law enforcement.

Abortion-rights measures failed 2 years ago in Florida and South Dakota.

Transgender Restrictions Pass in Some States

Nebraska voters approved an amendment to add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution. And in Arizona, voters passed a measure that extends public school sports restrictions to private schools.

Voters in Colorado and Washington also were considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump's administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.

Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. In the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington, the measures were placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors.

#5680. Humana, athenahealth collaborate on expanded electronic prior authorizations nationwide

Humana, athenahealth collaborate on expanded electronic prior authorizations nationwide" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana and athenahealth are expanding electronic prior authorizations nationwide in a newly announced collaboration.

Through athenaPayer, Humana is able to connect with over 180,000 providers across the athenaOne network, which the partners said will create a more connected experience between the health plan and clinicians.

“Every phone call, fax and portal log-in adds work for a practice trying to get a patient the care they need,” said Paul Brient, athenahealth chief product and operations officer, in a statement. “Prior authorization shouldn’t require care teams to navigate a different process for every health plan. By connecting health plans and practices through one solution with a common workflow, we’re creating a more scalable way to exchange information, reducing work for both providers and payers while, most importantly, helping patients access care faster.”

Athenahealth internal data show more than 6,000 providers processed nearly 35,000 electronic prior authorizations with Humana in September, with over 70% completed without requiring additional information from staff.

The collaboration reflects Humana’s broader strategy to improve care access by requiring fewer prior authorizations and making the process simpler when needed, executives said.

“Our goal is straightforward: help people get the right care at the right time while reducing unnecessary burden on the physicians and care teams who serve them,” said Traci Granston, M.D., Humana vice president of clinical innovation and trend, in a statement. “… This collaboration with athenahealth is another step forward, ensuring that providers spend less time navigating administrative processes and more time focused on patient care.”

In June 2025, insurers nationwide—including Humana—agreed to take steps to reform prior authorization, including supporting electronic prior authorizations.
